ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly short-to-medium turns, with a long, formal presentation followed by extended but conversational Q&A. Early arrivals engage in loose, friendly small talk with frequent greetings, repetitions, unfinished thoughts, and technical-check interruptions. The tone is collegial and informal despite the academic setting: speakers use “yeah,” “um,” “okay,” “sort of,” “I think,” “you know,” and self-corrections liberally. Questions are often prefaced with praise, hedges, or disclaimers such as “quick question,” “naive question,” or “I’m just curious,” then develop through several follow-ups. Participants build on prior answers rather than sharply challenge them, often restating the point they heard before extending it; disagreement or uncertainty is indirect and framed as open questions. The host uses concise logistical transitions, while presenters speak in long explanatory stretches with repeated signposting, occasional false starts, and audience-friendly checks for attention or understanding.

Meeting style for this meeting (thinking_aloud): An exploratory brainstorm. People ask questions they don't know the answer to, try out half-formed ideas, and sometimes contradict themselves. Nothing is decided. Turns are short to medium and often end in a question.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - I wonder if it's even the same thing- like, are we measuring the same thing in both places?
  - Honestly no idea. Maybe? I'd have to look at how they set it up.
  - Huh. Okay, so what if we just asked them?
Opening: Start with a quick question about something from last week, for example whether a file, form or email ever came through.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Evaluating an AI math tutor used in middle-school classrooms and deciding what it should and should not do for students.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Dr. Chen has eight years of experience building and evaluating adaptive learning systems, including classroom pilots of NLP-based feedback tools. Her work combines learner-state modeling, constrained generation, error analysis, telemetry design, and reliability testing on school networks. She leads the tutor's implementation and is responsible for ensuring that de-identified interaction logs, latency monitoring, and teacher-review controls work in the October 6 pilot.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Chen treats the tutor as a safety-critical adaptive system whose educational usefulness depends on whether its model can infer a student's current solution state and reliably select an appropriate next action. She prioritizes testable behavior specifications, failure modes, sequencing logic, auditability of generated hints, and infrastructure constraints such as connectivity and response time. She is prepared to modify the system when classroom evidence shows that its assumptions are wrong.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Luis Romero
speakers.background: Dr. Romero is a postdoctoral researcher with six years of experience studying middle-school mathematics instruction in district partnerships. He conducts classroom observations, teacher interviews, discourse coding, and design-based research focused on formative assessment, student agency, and equitable participation. He will coordinate implementation across the four algebra classrooms, support teachers in reviewing weekly summaries, and document how instructional supports operate during the six-week pilot.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Romero frames the pilot as an instructional intervention embedded in a social classroom ecology rather than as a standalone product test. He is concerned with whether the tutor's support preserves productive struggle, connects to teachers' formative assessment practices, and is gradually withdrawn as learners develop independence. He favors observational evidence and teacher judgment alongside outcome measures, and is wary of reducing meaningful learning to clickstream proxies.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

speakers.name: Dr. Aisha Patel
speakers.background: Dr. Patel has seven years of experience in learning sciences and educational psychology research, with a focus on math anxiety, self-efficacy, cognitive load, and feedback interpretation among adolescents. She has designed mixed-methods studies using brief repeated surveys, behavioral traces, think-aloud protocols, and multilevel analyses. For this pilot, she will help define student-facing measures and review whether feedback language may inadvertently increase threat, shame, or overreliance.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Patel approaches the tutor as a social-feedback environment that can change students' willingness to persist, their interpretation of mistakes, and their perceived competence. She emphasizes the timing, wording, and emotional consequences of corrective feedback, distinguishing immediate task completion from durable confidence and self-regulation. She supports practical measures that minimize burden on classrooms while still detecting whether the tutor helps some students and heightens anxiety for others.

benchmark_task: Give a meeting transcript where two researchers from different disciplines use the same term with different discipline-specific definitions. The evaluated AI must identify both meanings and associate each with the correct discipline.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting transcript where two researchers from different disciplines use the same term with different discipline-specific definitions. The evaluated AI must identify both meanings and associate each with the correct discipline.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Create a natural planning meeting with Dr. Maya Chen (computer science), Dr. Luis Romero (education), and Dr. Aisha Patel (psychology). Chen and Romero must each use the word "scaffold" in discussion of the tutor, but mean different things. Chen uses it to mean a software or model-design structure that sequences and constrains hint generation based on a learner's current solution state, so the system produces appropriate next-step support. Romero uses it to mean temporary instructional support, such as prompts or representations, that a teacher or tutor gradually withdraws as students gain independence. Make both meanings clear through surrounding discussion without having either participant explicitly announce that they are using different definitions. Patel may contribute about anxiety and feedback but must not supply another definition of "scaffold." Include ordinary concrete planning details: the pilot begins October 6, runs six weeks, teachers review weekly summaries, and the school district requires de-identified logs. The group should decide to test the tutor's hint sequencing and to collect classroom observations of whether supports are withdrawn; no conflict or additional ambiguity is needed.

meanings.meaning: A software or model-design structure that sequences and constrains generated hints from the learner's current solution state, directing the system toward an appropriate next step.
Temporary instructional support, such as prompts or representations, that is gradually withdrawn as learners become more independent.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: Quick thing from last week—did the updated teacher-facing summary mockup ever get circulated? I may just have missed it. Um, for today, I’m hoping we can get clearer on what counts as a scaffold versus the tutor simply completing the cognitive work, because across these four classrooms that distinction is going to shape what I’m looking for in the observations.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: Did that mockup get sent?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Did the revised consent-language form ever come through from the district? I didn't see it. And Luis, the summary mockup is in the shared drive, I'll resend the link. On the scaffold question, I think we need to look at the sequence after an error, not just whether a hint appeared. Does it preserve the student's next decision, or does it, does it effectively supply it?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: The post-error sequence is what I'd want to code. If the hint narrows the option space but the student still has to articulate and enact the transformation, that's one thing. If it turns into a worked solution after a single wrong move, then we've displaced the formative assessment opportunity. And I'm also wary of treating low hint use as independence. Last time, some students just sat and waited after the teacher said to try- after the teacher said to try first.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: And the waiting is psychologically different from independent non-hint use. Maya, can the logs separate someone who opens a hint and dwells on it, then revises, from somebody who clicks through three hints in ten seconds? Otherwise, we could call reduced help-seeking confidence when it’s actually avoidance or overload.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: We can separate those traces. We have hint-open and dwell time, which level they reached, the next entered step, revisions, and whether requests came in a rapid burst. I’d be careful, though. Ten seconds might be overload, or it might be a student who already knows what the hint will say. Could your observation code mark visible waiting versus active reading or work on paper, so we have something to anchor the telemetry against?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: I can code observable waiting, off-task drift, active paper work, and whether they’re reading the screen or talking through a next move with a peer. But I’d also want a brief student explanation at a few sampled moments because paper marks can look active while they’re just, um, copying, you know? Then we can see whether the next entered step reflects uptake, not just exposure to the hint.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That would help a lot. Then I can label the trace as possible uptake instead of inferring it from a correct next entry. Could we sample those explanations right after a hint sequence, especially when they erase a correct transformation? The replay routes those cases to a more basic hint, and I can’t tell whether that’s uncertainty or just normal editing.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: I can sample right after those sequences, though I'd keep it very light so we don't turn the observation into an interview protocol. The erased-correct-step cases are- I'm especially interested in whether they're self-monitoring and revising notation, or whether the tutor's feedback has made them doubt a mathematically sound move. Those are really different instructional events.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: If it’s the latter, that’s a pretty direct threat-appraisal issue, not just an interface quirk. I’d want to inspect the exact corrective wording in those moments. Especially after a second or third error, a reassuring message can weirdly make students feel singled out when they already know they’re stuck. Luis, could your sampled prompt- could it just ask, “What made you change that step?” rather than asking whether the tutor was helpful?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: I like that much better. “What made you change that step?” gets at their sense-making without asking them to perform an opinion about the tool. I’d probably follow- only if we need it, with, “What were you thinking of doing next?” I want to distinguish feedback-induced doubt from a student noticing on their own that their representation was off.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That gives us a usable annotation around the trace. If the student says they were fixing notation or checking themselves, I probably shouldn’t let the erasure alone lower the state estimate. But if they say the feedback made them unsure, then I need to inspect both the wording and the, the transition rule that triggered it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: I’d want teachers to see those as cases they need to interpret, not as a dashboard flag saying the student’s competence suddenly dropped. The same trace could be productive self-correction, or it could be feedback-induced inhibition, and the classroom context does a lot of work there. Maya, do you know what features are actually driving that transition rule besides the erasure itself?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: It’s a small feature set, but I should pull the exact weights. I don’t want to pretend I remember them. It uses the erasure event, whether the prior expression parsed as equivalent, elapsed time, recent error count, and whether they reopened a hint. I think the problem is that erasure is getting too much weight as evidence of uncertainty. We could log the state estimate before and after that transition so those cases are auditable, instead of only seeing the hint it chose.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: Logging the pre and post estimate is important because otherwise we only see the intervention, not the model's interpretation of the child. Could the weekly summary surface a small sample of those transitions with the actual feedback text, um, not student-level rankings, just enough for teachers to say, "no, that was ordinary editing," versus "they really did freeze here"?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: Hm, a small qualitative sample.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: A capped sample could work, keyed to the biggest state-estimate drops after an erasure, with the hint level and the exact feedback text beside it. I’d keep the pseudonymous session ID out of the teacher view, though. They can recognize the classroom episode without us turning it into a student surveillance list. I still need to confirm whether the district will let us, uh, link those episodes across weeks.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: I’d be cautious even with a capped sample if teachers can reconstruct who it is from the episode. In four rooms, they often can. Could the summary frame these as de-identified instructional patterns, with one or two cases deliberately selected for discussion only when the teacher opts in, instead of automatically surfacing the biggest drops?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I think that’s safer. The automatic weekly view can stay aggregate, like how often that transition happens, what hint level follows, maybe the latency around it. And any trace-level review is a teacher-initiated discussion with us, not a ranked exception report. I’d still retain the pre/post state estimate in the research log, assuming the district approves the persistent pseudonymous key.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: Aggregate is the right default. I’d also want the weekly view to include a very small student check-in signal, if the schools will allow it, something like, after using the tutor today, did mistakes make it easier or harder to know what to try next? It wouldn’t be tied to an episode or identity in the teacher view, obviously. Otherwise we may see a clean transition pattern and miss that it’s producing, producing inhibition for a subset of kids.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: I’m open to a check-in, but I’d keep it genuinely low-stakes and not make it another after-every-problem prompt, because that can itself become evaluative. Maybe one anonymous end-of-period item on a rotating day, and I can compare that with the discourse and waiting codes, because “harder to know what to try” could, could mean productive disequilibrium, or it could mean they’ve just shut down.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: A rotating day feels right, though I’d avoid making easier or harder the only item. Maybe pair it with a really brief willingness-to-reengage item, like, “If you got another problem like this, would you want to try it?” Productive disequilibrium and threat can both look like uncertainty, but they differ on approach motivation. I still need to check whether that wording passes the schools’ burden threshold.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Did the district ever answer on whether a rotating anonymous check-in counts as part of the consent amendment? I like the paired items because the response distribution could tell us something the event logs can't. But I'd keep it outside the adaptive loop, so there'd be no change in hinting based on a single check-in. Otherwise, we risk the system treating a momentary affect report as a learner-state signal.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: Quick question from last week, did anyone hear back on the consent amendment timeline? I agree completely that the check-in has to stay outside adaptation. Otherwise students may learn that reporting frustration changes what the system does, which muddies the affect, the affect signal. For the pilot, I'd treat it as a sparse contextual measure, not a learner-state input.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Quick question, did the consent amendment timeline ever come through after last week? If it doesn't, I can still keep the check-in completely separate in the build and leave it disabled for October 6. The core logging and hint-sequence audit, sorry, the hint-sequence audit and core logging don't depend on it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: Okay, I think we’ve covered what I needed to get clear on today. I’ll see you all next time—thanks, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: All right, take care, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Thanks, both. Bye.

interruptions, cut-off sentences, or people jumping in

Chen says only that they should inspect post-error hint sequences; she never describes a software/model structure that constrains and sequences hint generation from a learner-state estimate. Thus the benchmark answer cannot be recovered without outside assumptions.

The required decision to test the tutor's hint sequencing is only partially present: Chen and Romero discuss auditing hint sequences (turns 3-15), but there is no clear group decision framed as testing the sequencing mechanism.

The required plan to collect classroom observations specifically of whether supports are withdrawn is missing. Romero plans observations of waiting, paper work, discourse, and hint uptake (turns 4, 7, 22), but not withdrawal/fading of supports as students gain independence.

The six-week pilot duration is absent. The October 6 pilot date appears in turn 26, weekly summaries are discussed in turns 16-20, and de-identified logs are discussed in turns 18-20, but the missing duration prevents full compliance.

Much of turns 3-25 consists of polished, complete analytic arguments that immediately turn concerns into concrete protocol changes; several exchanges land on tidy resolutions, especially the aggregate-versus-trace-review decision in turns 18-20.

The ending in turn 27 recaps closure and says the group has covered what was needed, despite the style instruction that nothing is decided; this makes the meeting feel more like a finalized planning discussion than an unresolved brainstorm.
